title: There's nothing new in this CPD...and that's a good thing hats-a-good-thing/
author: Paul Cline
summary: Paul Cline argues teachers should stop treating "nothing new" as a disappointing verdict on a CPD session and instead reframe professional development around two questions applied to existing practice: can I do it better, and can I do it more? He works through familiar techniques -- retrieval practice, modelling, examples and non-examples, and success criteria -- showing for each how a teacher might refine or extend something they already do, rather than bolt on an unfamiliar new initiative. Cline gives four reasons this approach works better than introducing novelty: new ideas force teachers to focus on mechanics rather than underlying principles; small refinements to existing practice can have outsized impact (asking a cold-call question, pausing, then naming the student); reflecting on existing routines can improve how they're explained to students; and regular review keeps ideas fresh and builds a shared staff vocabulary as personnel change. He closes with a sports analogy -- Roger Federer's coach wouldn't teach him a new stroke, but would fine-tune his backhand -- to argue that treating refinement as legitimate CPD, rather than an admission of stagnation, is what taking teaching seriously as a profession actually looks like.
points: Cline reframes CPD around two questions for existing practice -- can I do it better, can I do it more -- rather than treating the absence of a new idea as a failed session.

He argues new ideas force teachers to focus on mechanics ("what does it look like") at the expense of underlying principles ("what is it for"), which can lead to superficial adoption that looks right but doesn't work.
A concrete example of refinement: pausing between a cold-call question and naming the student, rather than naming the student first, can meaningfully change participation ratio.

Cline's closing analogy -- Federer's coach wouldn't teach him a new stroke but would fine-tune his backhand -- reframes refinement-focused CPD as a mark of professional seriousness rather than a lack of ambition.
quotes: Professional development is both an entitlement and a responsibility – it’s literally written in the teacher standards.
Instead I think there are two things we should be thinking about and taking from CPD when it's stuff I already know: Can I do it better? Can I do it more?
The very simple refinement of asking the question, pausing, and then naming the student could have a big impact on participation ratio.
Roger Federer wouldn’t expect his coach to suddenly give him a new stroke to learn, but he wouldn’t mind being given suggestions for how to improve his backhand.
Experts in other fields have no reservations about being asked to fine-tune their practice and, if we want to be taken seriously as a profession, neither should we.
